rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The squashfs file system type is a compressed, read-only Linux file system embedded in small systems (similar to cramfs). squashfs images can be used without first unpacking them.
rules.impact: Removing support for unnecessary file system types reduces the likelihood of system compromise. If this file system type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The udf file system type is the Universal Disk Format used to implement the ISO/IEC 13346 and ECMA-167 specifications. It is an open-vendor file system type for storing data on a wide variety of media. This file system type is required to support DVD writing and newer optical disc formats.
rules.impact: Removing support for unnecessary file system types reduces the likelihood of system compromise. If this file system type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /tmp is configured
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-writable directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp directory is world-writable, there is a risk of resource exhaustion if it is not bound to a separate partition. In addition, giving /tmp its own file system allows the administrator to set the noexec mount option, making /tmp useless for an attacker installing executable code. It also prevents an attacker from creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated. Once the program is updated, the hard link is broken and the attacker has their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability is found in the program, the attacker can continue to exploit the known flaw.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot attempt to create block or character special devices in /tmp.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable files.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot execute binary files from /tmp.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /tmp.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var is configured
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and other system services for temporary storage of dynamic data. Some directories created by these processes may be writable.
rules.impact: Because the /var directory can contain writable files and directories, there is a resource-exhaustion risk if it is not on a separate partition.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var file system is intended only for variable files such as logs, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var /tmp is configured
rules.explanation: The /var/tmp directory is a writable directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp directory is world-writable, there is a risk of resource exhaustion if it is not bound to a separate partition. In addition, giving /var/tmp its own file system allows the administrator to set the noexec option on the mount, making /var/tmp useless for an attacker installing executable code. It also prevents an attacker from creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated. Once the program is updated, the hard link is broken and the attacker has their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability is found in the program, the attacker can continue to exploit the known flaw.

rules.title: The noexec parameter is set on the /var/tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot execute files from /var/tmp.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var/tmp.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/tmp partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/tmp file system is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot attempt to create block or character special devices in /var/tmp.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log is configured
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data.
rules.impact: There are two important reasons to ensure that system logs are stored on a separate partition: protection against resource exhaustion (because logs can become quite large) and protection of audit data.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/log partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var/log.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/log partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log file system is intended only for log files, set this option so that users cannot execute binary files from /var/log.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/log partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log filesystem is intended only for log files, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var/log.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon stores log data in the /var/log/audit directory.
rules.impact: There are two important reasons to Ensure that data collected by auditd is stored on a separate partition: protection against resource exhaustion (because the audit.log file can become quite large) and protection of audit data. The audit daemon calculates how much free space remains and takes action based on the results. If other processes (for example, syslog) consume space on the same partition as auditd, it may not operate as intended.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /var/log/audit partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log/audit filesystem is intended only for audit logs, set this option so that users cannot run executable binaries from /var/log/audit.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /var/log/audit partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log/audit filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var/log/audit.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /var/log/audit partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option specifies that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Because the /var/log/audit filesystem is intended only for variable files such as logs, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var/log/audit.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and system services for dynamic and temporary data. Some directories under /var may be world-writable.
rules.impact: Placing /var on a separate partition enables additional mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage exploits. Isolation also helps contain growth of variable data so it does not exhaust the root filesystem.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var is intended for variable data such as logs and service state, applying nosuid prevents creation of setuid binaries under /var that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The nodev option is set on the /dev/shm partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain special devices.
rules.impact: Because the /dev/shm filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option so that users cannot attempt to create special devices on /dev/shm partitions.

rules.title: The noexec option is set on the /dev/shm partition is configured
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable files.
rules.impact: Setting this option on the file system prevents users from executing programs from shared memory. This keeps users from introducing potentially malicious software into the system.

rules.title: The nosuid option is set on the /dev/shm partition is configured
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain setuid files.
rules.impact: Setting this option on a file system prevents users from introducing privileged programs onto the system and prevents non-root users from executing them.

rules.title: Automounting is disabled
rules.explanation: Autofs automatically mounts devices, including CD/DVD and USB drives.
rules.impact: With automatic mounting enabled, anyone with physical access can attach a USB drive or disk and have its contents available on the system even if they were not permitted to mount it.

rules.title: GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: Most package managers use GPG key signing to verify package integrity during installation.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure updates are obtained from a valid source to protect against spoofing that could result in accidental installation of malware on the system.

rules.title: Gpgcheck is enabled globally
rules.explanation: The gpgcheck parameter, located in the main section of /etc/yum.conf and in individual /etc/yum/repos.d/*.repo files, determines whether the RPM package signature is verified before installation.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that the RPM package signature is always verified before installation to guarantee that the software is obtained from a trusted source.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Systems must be configured with appropriate package manager repositories so that the system can receive the latest patches and updates.
rules.impact: If system package repositories are configured incorrectly, important patches may not be identified, or a rogue repository may contain compromised software.
rules.scope: Parameter for active and current repositories

rules.title: AIDE is installed is configured
rules.explanation: AIDE takes a snapshot of file system state, including modification times, permissions, and file hashes, which can then be compared with the current file system state to detect system changes.
rules.impact: By monitoring file system state, compromised files can be detected to prevent or limit the possibility of accidental or malicious misconfigurations or modified binaries.

rules.title: File system integrity is checked regularly is configured
rules.explanation: Periodic file system integrity checking is required to detect changes in the file system.
rules.impact: Periodic file checking allows a system administrator to regularly determine whether important files have been modified in an unauthorized manner.

rules.title: The bootloader password is set is configured
rules.explanation: Setting a bootloader password will require anyone rebooting the system to enter a password before setting boot parameters from the command line.
rules.impact: Requiring a bootloader password at startup will prevent unauthorized entry of boot parameters or modification of the boot partition by an unauthorized user. This prevents weakening of user security (for example, disabling SELinux at boot).

rules.title: Bootloader configuration permissions are configured
rules.explanation: The grub configuration file contains boot settings and passwords for unlocking boot options. The grub2 configuration is typically located in /boot/grub2/grub.cfg. In newer grub2, the encrypted bootloader password is contained in /boot/grub2/user.cfg.
rules.impact: Setting permissions to read and write for the root user only prevents non-root users from viewing or modifying boot parameters. Non-root users who read boot parameters may identify security weaknesses at boot time and exploit them.
rules.scope: The Access parameter in /boot/grub2/grub.cfg and permissions on /boot/grub2/grubenv

rules.title: Kernel dump storage is disabled
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is typically used to determine the cause of a program abort. It can also be used to collect confidential information from the core file.
rules.impact: A core dump includes a memory image created at the moment the operating system terminates an application. The memory image may contain sensitive data and is generally useful only to developers attempting to debug issues.

rules.title: Core dumps are restricted is configured
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is typically used to determine why a program was aborted. It can also be used to collect sensitive information from the core file. The system provides the ability to set a soft limit for core dumps, but it can be changed by the user.
rules.impact: Setting a hard limit for core dumps prevents users from overriding the soft limit. If core dumps are required, consider setting limits for user groups (see limits.conf(5)). In addition, setting the fs.suid_dumpable variable to 0 will prevent setuid programs from dumping core.
rules.scope: Parameters hard core and fs\.suid_dumpable in /etc/security/limits.conf or /etc/security/limits.d/*

rules.title: Address space layout randomization (ASLR) is enabled
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is an exploit-mitigation technique that randomly arranges the address space of key process data areas.
rules.impact: Randomizing virtual memory region placement makes memory-page exploits harder to write because memory layout continually changes.

rules.title: SELinux is installed is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux provides mandatory access control.
rules.impact: Without a mandatory access control system in place, only the standard access control system will be available.

rules.title: SELinux is not disabled in the bootloader configuration is configured
rules.explanation: Configure SELinux to be enabled at boot and ensure that it has not been overridden by GRUB boot parameters.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot in your GRUB configuration to ensure that the controls it provides will not be overridden.
rules.scope: The SELINUX parameter in /etc/selinux/config; the selinux and enforcing parameters in /etc/default/grub

rules.title: The SELinux policy is configured
rules.explanation: Configure SELinux to meet or exceed the default targeted policy, which confines only daemons and system software.
rules.impact: Security configuration requirements vary. Some sites may mandate a policy that is stricter than the default policy, which is entirely acceptable. This item is intended to ensure that at least the default recommendations are met.

rules.title: SELinux mode is not disabled is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux can operate in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing: • Enforcing — the default and recommended operating mode; in enforcing mode SELinux operates normally, applying the loaded security policy across the entire system. • Permissive — the system acts as if SELinux is applying the loaded security policy, including labeling objects and creating access-denial entries in the logs, but does not actually deny any operations. Although this is not recommended for production systems, permissive mode can be useful for SELinux policy development. • Disabled — strongly not recommended; the system not only avoids applying the SELinux policy, but also avoids labeling any persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux in the future more difficult.
rules.impact: Running SELinux in disabled mode is strongly discouraged; the system not only avoids enforcing SELinux policy but also avoids labeling any persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux later more difficult.

rules.title: The SELinux state is enforcing is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux can be in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, enforcing. Enforcing is the recommended default operating mode; in enforcing mode SELinux applies the loaded security policy to the entire system. Permissive - the system acts as if SELinux is applying the loaded security policy, including labeling objects and creating access-denial entries in the logs, but does not actually deny any operations. Although permissive mode is not recommended for production systems, it can be useful for SELinux policy development. Disabled is strongly not recommended; the system not only avoids enforcing the SELinux policy, but also avoids labeling any persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux in the future more difficult.
rules.impact: SELinux must be enabled at boot time to ensure that the controls it provides are continuously in effect.

rules.title: Unrestricted services do not exist is configured
rules.explanation: Unconfined processes run in unconfined domains.
rules.impact: Unconfined processes are subject to SELinux policy rules, but there are policy rules that allow processes running in unconfined domains nearly all access. Processes running in unconfined domains fall back to using DAC rules exclusively. If an unconfined process is compromised, SELinux does not prevent an attacker from accessing system resources and data, but DAC rules are still applied. SELinux is a security enhancement on top of DAC rules, not a replacement for them.

rules.title: SETroubleshoot is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The SETroubleshoot service notifies of SELinux denials through a convenient interface. The service provides important information about configuration errors, unauthorized intrusions, and other potential errors.
rules.impact: The SETroubleshoot service is an unnecessary daemon running on a server, especially if X Windows is disabled.

rules.title: The MCS translation service (mcstrans) is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The mcstransd daemon provides category label information to client processes that request information. Label translations are defined in /etc/selinux/targeted/setrans.conf.
rules.impact: Because this service is used infrequently, remove it to reduce the amount of potentially vulnerable code running on the system.

rules.title: The message of the day is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after login and function as a message of the day for authenticated users. Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at login. This information can be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following options, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users who attempt to log on of their legal status with respect to the system and should contain the name of the organization that owns the system and any applicable monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch-level information in logon banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to target specific system exploits. Authorized users can easily obtain this information by running the command "uname -a" after logging on.

rules.title: The local login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log in on local terminals. Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at login. This information may be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following options, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users who attempt to log on of their legal status with respect to the system and should contain the name of the organization that owns the system and any applicable monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch-level information in logon banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to target specific system exploits. Authorized users can easily obtain this information by running the command "uname -a" after logging on.

rules.title: The remote login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before logon for remote connections from configured services. Unix systems have typically displayed OS release and patch-level information at logon. This information can be useful to developers who develop software for a specific OS platform. If mingetty supports the following parameters, they display operating system information: \m - machine architecture \r - operating system release \s - operating system name \v - operating system version.
rules.impact: Warning messages inform users who attempt to log on of their legal status with respect to the system and should contain the name of the organization that owns the system and any applicable monitoring policies. Displaying OS and patch-level information in logon banners also has the side effect of providing detailed system information to attackers attempting to target specific system exploits. Authorized users can easily obtain this information by running the command "uname -a" after logging on.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/motd are configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after logon and function as the message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: If /etc/motd does not have the correct owner, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/issue are configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log on to local terminals.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue does not have the correct owner, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/issue.net are configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before login for remote connections from configured services.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue.net does not have the correct owner, it can be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: The GNOME display manager is removed is configured
rules.explanation: The GNOME Display Manager (GDM) is a program that manages graphical display servers and handles graphical user logins.
rules.impact: If a graphical user interface (GUI) is not required, it should be removed to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: The GDM login banner is configured
rules.explanation: GDM is the GNOME Display Manager, which manages graphical login for GNOME-based systems.
rules.impact: Warning banners inform users attempting to log on of their legal status with respect to the system and should include the name of the organization that owns the system and any applicable monitoring policies.

rules.title: GDM screen locks cannot be overridden is configured
rules.explanation: GNOME Desktop Manager can automatically lock the screen when a user has been idle for a period of time. Using lock mode in dconf, you can prevent users from changing certain settings. To lock a dconf key or subpath, create a locks subdirectory in the key-file directory. Files in this directory contain a list of keys or nested paths to lock. As with key files, you can add any number of files to this directory.
rules.impact: Setting a lock value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized user access to another user's unattended session. Without locking system settings, user settings take precedence over system settings.

rules.title: Updates, patches, and additional security software are installed is configured
rules.explanation: Patches are periodically released for installed software either due to security flaws or to add additional functionality.
rules.impact: Newer patches may contain security improvements that will not be available after the latest full update. As a result, it is recommended to use the most recent software patches to take advantage of the newest functionality. As with any software installation, organizations need to determine whether a given update meets their requirements and verify compatibility and support of any additional software with the selected update version.

rules.title: The system-wide cryptographic policy is not set to legacy is configured
rules.explanation: System-wide crypto policies followed by core cryptography components allow algorithms to be consistently deprecated and disabled across the entire system.
rules.impact: If the system-wide Legacy crypto policy is selected, it includes support for TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and SSH2 or later. DSA, 3DES, and RC4 algorithms are allowed, while RSA and Diffie-Hellman parameters are accepted if they are greater than 1023 bits. These legacy protocols and algorithms can make the system vulnerable to attacks, including those listed in RFC 7457.

rules.title: Time synchronization is used is configured
rules.explanation: System time should be synchronized among all systems in the environment. This is typically done by establishing an authoritative time server or set of servers, and all systems synchronize their clocks to them.
rules.impact: Time synchronization is important to support time-sensitive security mechanisms such as Kerberos, and also ensures that log files have consistent timestamps across the enterprise, which aids forensic investigations.

rules.title: Chrony is configured
rules.explanation: Chrony is a daemon that implements the Network Time Protocol (NTP), intended to synchronize system clocks across various systems and use a source that is highly accurate. chrony can be configured as a client and/or a server.
rules.impact: If the system uses chrony, correct configuration is vital to ensure time synchronization operates properly. This recommendation applies only if the system uses chrony.

rules.title: Xinetd is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: EXtended InterNET Daemon (xinetd) is an open-source super-daemon that replaced the original inetd daemon. The xinetd daemon listens for well-known services and launches the appropriate daemon to correctly respond to service requests.
rules.impact: If xinetd services are not required, it is recommended to disable the daemon.

rules.title: The Avahi server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: Avahi is a free zeroconf implementation that includes a system for multicast DNS/DNS-SD service discovery. Avahi allows programs to publish and discover services and hosts running on a local network without a specific configuration. For example, a user can connect a computer to the network and Avahi will automatically find printers to print to, files to browse, people to communicate with, and network services running on the machine.
rules.impact: Automatic discovery of network services is typically not required for system functionality. It is recommended to disable the service to reduce the likelihood of attack.

rules.title: CUPS is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Common Unix Printing System (CUPS) allows printing to both local and network printers. A system running CUPS can also accept print jobs from remote systems and print them on local printers. It also provides the ability to administer the service remotely over the web.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to print jobs or accept print jobs from other systems, it is recommended to disable CUPS to reduce attack likelihood.

rules.title: The DHCP server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) is a service that allows machines to be assigned IP addresses dynamically.
rules.impact: If the system is not specifically configured to operate as a DHCP server, it is recommended to disable this service to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The DNS server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The Domain Name System (DNS) is a hierarchical naming system that maps names to IP addresses of computers, services, and other resources connected to a network.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically intended to operate as a DNS server, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack likelihood.

rules.title: The FTP server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between network hosts. FTP authentication is transmitted in cleartext.
rules.impact: FTP does not provide confidentiality or integrity for data in transit. It is recommended to use a secure file transfer protocol. If an FTP server is not required, it should be removed.

rules.title: The FTP server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) allows networked computers to transfer files between a server and clients over a network where authentication is absent (disallow anonymous user connections to the server).
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or credentials. It is recommended to use sftp if file transfer is required. If there is no need to run the system as an FTP server (for example, to allow anonymous downloads), it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The TFTP server is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP computers. TFTP servers allow a TFTP client to connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. This allows an attacker to easily use TFTP to obtain access to files.

rules.title: The HTTP server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: HTTP or web servers provide the ability to host website content.
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as a web server, it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: Unused IMAP and POP3 server is not disabled is configured
rules.explanation: Dovecot is an open-source IMAP and POP3 server for Linux-based systems used by default.
rules.impact: If POP3 and/or IMAP servers are not provided on this system, it is recommended that the service be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: Samba is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Samba daemon allows system administrators to configure their Linux systems to share filesystems and directories with Windows desktops. Samba will advertise filesystems and directories via the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. Windows desktop users will be able to mount these directories and filesystems as drive letters on their systems.
rules.impact: If there is no need to mount directories and file systems to Windows systems, this service can be disabled to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The HTTP proxy server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: Squid is a standard proxy server used in many distributions.
rules.impact: If a proxy server is not required, it is recommended to disable the squid proxy server to reduce the likelihood of a potential attack.

rules.title: The SNMP server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) server is used to listen for SNMP, execute commands, or collect information and then send the results back to the requesting system.
rules.impact: An SNMP server can communicate using SNMP v1, which transmits data in plaintext and does not require authentication to execute commands. If SNMP is not required, it is recommended that the SNMP service not be used. If SNMP is required, the server should be configured to prohibit the use of SNMP v1.

rules.title: The NIS server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The ypserv package provides the Network Information Service (NIS). NIS is a client-server system for distributing system configuration files. An NIS server is a set of programs that enable distribution of configuration files.
rules.impact: The NIS service is inherently an insecure system that has been vulnerable to DoS attacks, buffer overflows, and poor authentication for NIS map queries. NIS has generally been replaced by protocols such as Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). It is recommended to disable the service and use other, more secure services.

rules.title: The Telnet server is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The telnet-server package contains the telnet daemon, which accepts connections from users of other systems via the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Using unencrypted transmission may allow a user with access to network traffic analysis to steal sensitive data.

rules.title: The mail transfer agent is configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: Mail transfer agents (MTAs), such as sendmail and Postfix, are used to listen for incoming mail and deliver messages to the appropriate user or mail server. If a mail server is not used on the system, it is recommended that the MTA be configured to process local mail only.
rules.impact: The MTA daemon should not listen on a port unless the server is intended to be a mail server that receives and processes mail from other systems.

rules.title: NFS and RPC are not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The Network File System (NFS) is one of the earliest and most common file systems in the UNIX environment. It provides the ability for systems to mount file systems of other servers over the network.
rules.impact: If the system does not export NFS shares or act as an NFS client, it is recommended to disable these services to reduce the likelihood of a remote attack.

rules.title: Rpcbind is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The rpcbind utility maps RPC services to the ports they listen on. RPC processes notify rpcbind at startup, registering the ports they listen on and the RPC program numbers they expect to serve. A client system then contacts rpcbind on the server with a specific RPC program number. The rpcbind service redirects the client to the correct port number so it can contact the requested service. Portmapper is an RPC service that always listens on TCP and UDP 111 and is used to map other RPC services (such as nfs, nlockmgr, quotad, mountd, and so on) to the corresponding port number on the server. When a remote host makes an RPC call to this server, it first consults portmap to determine where the RPC server is listening.
rules.impact: A small request (~82 bytes over UDP) sent to Portmapper generates a large response (amplification of 7x to 28x), making it a suitable tool for DDoS attacks. If rpcbind is not required, it is recommended that the rpcbind package be removed to reduce the system's likelihood of attack.

rules.title: The rsync service is not enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The rsyncd service is used to synchronize files between systems over network channels.
rules.impact: The rsyncd service presents a security threat because it uses unencrypted protocols for communication.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: The telnet package contains the telnet client, which allows users to establish connections to other systems using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Unencrypted transmission may allow an unauthorized user to steal credentials.

rules.title: The LDAP client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) was introduced as a replacement for NIS/YP. It is a service that provides a method for looking up information from a central database.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to act as an LDAP client, it is recommended that it be removed to reduce the likelihood of attack.

rules.title: The TFTP client is not installed is configured
rules.explanation: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP computers. TFTP servers allow a TFTP client to connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. This allows an attacker to easily use TFTP to obtain access to files.

rules.title: Wi-Fi is disabled on the OS
rules.explanation: The operating system includes a set of wireless networking tools that allow system administrators to configure and use wireless networks.
rules.impact: If wireless communication is not used, wireless devices can be disabled to reduce a potential attack vector.

rules.title: IP forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.ip_forward flag is used to indicate whether the system may forward packets.
rules.impact: Setting the flag to 0 ensures that a multi-interface system can never forward packets and therefore will never serve as a router.
rules.scope: The net\.ipv4\.ip_forward parameter in /etc/sysctl.conf and /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf and /usr/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf or /run/sysctl.d/*.conf

rules.title: Packet forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: ICMP redirects are used to send routing information to other hosts. When the host itself is not acting as a router (host configuration), there is no need to send redirects.
rules.impact: An attacker can use a compromised host to send invalid ICMP redirects to another router in an attempt to disrupt routing and give users access to a system configured by the attacker rather than a legitimate system.
rules.scope: The net\.ipv4\.conf\.all\.send_redirects and net\.ipv4\.conf\.default\.send_redirects parameters in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: Source routed packets are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: In a network, source routing allows the sender to partially or fully specify the route packets take through the network. Conversely, packets that are not source-routed follow a path determined by routers on the network. In some cases, systems may not be routable or reachable from a given location (for example, private addresses versus Internet-routable addresses), and source-routed packets would therefore need to be used.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route and net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route to 0 disables the system's acceptance of source-routed packets. If source-routed packets were allowed, they could be used to gain access to the system's private addresses because the route can be specified.
rules.scope: The parameters net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route and net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route or net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and tell your host information for sending packets via an alternate path. This is a way to update your system's routing tables from outside. By setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0, the system will not accept ICMP redirect messages and therefore will not allow outsiders to update the system's routing tables.
rules.impact: Attackers can use forged ICMP redirect messages to maliciously alter the system routing table and force it to send packets to incorrect networks.
rules.scope: The net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects and net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects parameters, or net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects, in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are similar to ICMP redirects, except that they come from gateways listed in the default gateway list. These gateways are assumed to be known to your system and are likely to be trusted.
rules.impact: Even known gateways can still be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects to 0 protects the system from routing table updates from possibly compromised known gateways.
rules.scope: The net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects and net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects parameters in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: Suspicious packets are logged is configured
rules.explanation: When this feature is enabled, it logs packets with non-routable source addresses in the kernel log.
rules.impact: Enabling this feature and logging these packets allows an administrator to investigate the likelihood that an attacker is sending spoofed packets to the system under investigation.
rules.scope: Parameters net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians and net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: ICMP broadcast requests are ignored is configured
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts to 1 will cause the system to ignore all ICMP echo requests and timestamp requests to broadcast and multicast addresses.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP echo requests and timestamps with broadcast or multicast destinations for your network can be used to force your host to start (or participate in) a Smurf attack. A Smurf attack is based on an attacker sending a large number of ICMP messages with a spoofed source address. All hosts that receive this message and respond will send echo-reply messages back to the spoofed address. If many hosts respond to the packets, the volume of traffic on the network can increase significantly.
rules.scope: The net\.ipv4\.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts parameter in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf or /usr/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf or /run/sysctl.d/*.conf

rules.title: Logging of bogus responses by the kernel is prevented is configured
rules.explanation: Setting icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses to 1 prevents the kernel from logging bogus (RFC-1122-incompatible) responses to broadcast packets, preventing file systems from being filled with useless log messages.
rules.impact: Some routers (and some attackers) will send replies that violate RFC-1122 and attempt to fill the log filesystem with a large number of useless error messages.
rules.scope: The net\.ipv4\.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses parameter in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf or /usr/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf or /run/sysctl.d/*.conf

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 forces the Linux kernel to use reverse path filtering for a received packet to determine whether the packet was valid. Essentially, with reverse path filtering, if the return packet does not leave from the same interface from which the corresponding original packet arrived, the packet is dropped (and logged if log_martians is set).
rules.impact: Setting these flags is a good way to deter attackers from sending packets into your system that cannot be answered. However, this feature fails if asymmetric routing is used. That occurs when dynamic routing protocols (BGP, OSPF, etc.) are used on your system. If you use asymmetric routing on your system, you will not be able to enable this feature without breaking routing.
rules.scope: The net\.ipv4\.conf\.all\.rp_filter parameter in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf or /usr/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf or /run/sysctl.d/*.conf

rules.title: TCP SYN cookies are enabled is configured
rules.explanation: When the tcp_syncookies parameter is set, the kernel processes TCP SYN packets normally until the connection queue is full. At that point the SYN cookie feature is triggered, which does not use the SYN queue. Instead, the kernel simply replies to the SYN with a SYN|ACK, but includes a specially crafted TCP sequence number that encodes the source and destination IP addresses and port numbers, as well as the time the packet was sent. A legitimate connection will send the ACK packet of the three-way handshake with the specially crafted sequence number. This allows the system to verify that it received a valid response to the SYN cookie and to accept the connection even if there is no matching SYN in the queue.
rules.impact: Attackers use SYN attacks for denial of service; the targeted system receives many SYN packets without completing the three-way handshake. This quickly consumes slots in the kernel's half-open connection queue and prevents legitimate connections. SYN cookies allow the system to accept valid connections even while it is under a denial-of-service attack.
rules.scope: Parameter net\.ipv4\.tcp_syncookies in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf or /usr/lib/sysctl.d/*.conf or /run/sysctl.d/*.conf

rules.title: IPv6 router advertisements are not accepted is configured
rules.explanation: This setting disables the system's ability to accept IPv6 router advertisements.
rules.impact: It is recommended that systems not accept router advertisements, as they can be tricked into routing traffic to compromised machines. Setting static routes on the system (typically a single default route to a trusted router) protects the system from incorrect routes.
rules.scope: Parameters net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: Auditd is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Auditd is the userspace component of the Linux audit system. It is responsible for writing audit records to disk.
rules.impact: Capturing system events provides system administrators with information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: The Audit service is enabled
rules.explanation: Enable the auditd daemon to record system events.
rules.impact: Collection of system events provides system administrators with information that allows them to determine whether unauthorized access to their system is occurring.

rules.title: Auditd is enabled in grub
rules.explanation: Configure grub2 so that auditable processes can be audited even if they start before auditd starts.
rules.impact: Audit events must be captured for processes that start before audit so that potentially malicious activity cannot go unnoticed.

rules.title: The audit_backlog_limit parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel-level audit subsystem uses a socket buffer queue to store audit events. Whenever a new audit event arrives, it is recorded and prepared for addition to this queue. The kernel boot parameter audit_backlog_limit=N, where N represents the number of messages, ensures that the queue cannot grow beyond a certain size. If an audit event is recorded that would cause the queue to exceed this limit, a failure occurs that is handled according to the system configuration.
rules.impact: If an audit event is recorded that causes the queue to grow beyond audit_backlog_limit, a failure occurs, audit records are lost, and potentially malicious activity may go unnoticed.

rules.title: The audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: The max_log_file_action parameter determines how to handle an audit log file that reaches the maximum size. The keep_logs value will rotate logs but never delete old logs.
rules.impact: It is important that an appropriate log file size is defined so that logs do not impact the system and audit data is not lost.

rules.title: Audit logs are not deleted automatically is configured
rules.explanation: Configure the maximum audit log file size. Once the log reaches the maximum size, it is rotated and a new log file is started.
rules.impact: In high-security environments, the benefits of maintaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing audit history.

rules.title: The system is shut down when audit logs are full is configured
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon must be configured to halt the system when audit logs are full.
rules.impact: In a high-security context, the benefits of retaining a long audit history outweigh the cost of storing that history.
rules.scope: Parameters space_left_action, action_mail_acct, and admin_space_left_action in /etc/audit/auditd.conf

rules.title: Auditd rules for sudoers are configured
rules.explanation: Monitor scope changes for system administrators. If the system has been correctly configured to force system administrators to log in as themselves first and then use the sudo command to execute privileged commands, scope changes can be monitored. The /etc/sudoers file or files in /etc/sudoers.d will be written when the files or related attributes are changed. Audit records will be tagged with the identifier "scope".
rules.impact: Changes to /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d may indicate that an unauthorized change was made to the system administrator's scope of activity.

rules.title: Actions of another user are always logged is configured
rules.explanation: Sudo provides users with temporary elevated privileges to perform operations as the superuser or another user.
rules.impact: Creating an audit log of users with temporarily elevated privileges and the operations they performed is essential for reporting. Administrators may want to correlate events recorded in the audit trail with entries recorded in the sudo log file to verify that unauthorized commands were not executed.

rules.title: Events that modify the sudo log file are collected is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor the sudo log file. If the system has been correctly configured to disable use of the su command and to require all administrators to log in first and then use sudo to execute privileged commands, all administrator commands will be recorded in /var/log/sudo.log. Each time a command is executed, an audit event will be generated because /var/log/sudo.log will be opened for writing, and the executed administrative command will be written to the log.
rules.impact: Changes to /var/log/sudo.log indicate that an administrator executed a command or that the log file itself was tampered with. Administrators may want to correlate events recorded in the audit log with entries in /var/log/sudo.log to verify that unauthorized commands were not executed.

rules.title: Auditd rules for system date and time changes are configured
rules.explanation: Capture events when the system date and/or time were changed.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes to the system date and/or time may be an indication of malicious activity on the system.

rules.title: Use of privileged commands is collected is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor privileged programs that have the setuid and/or setgid bit set on execution to determine whether unprivileged users are executing these commands.
rules.impact: Execution of privileged commands by unprivileged users may indicate that someone is attempting to gain unauthorized access to the system.

rules.title: Unsuccessful file access attempts are collected is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor unsuccessful file access attempts. The following parameters are associated with system calls that manage files: • create — create • open — open, openat • truncation — truncate, ftruncate. An audit log record will be written only if all of the following criteria are met for the user when attempting to access a file: • unprivileged user (auid>=UID_MIN) • not a Daemon event (auid=4294967295/unset/-1) • if the system call returned EACCES (access denied) or EPERM (some other persistent error associated with the specific system call).
rules.impact: Failed attempts to open, create, or truncate files may indicate that a user or process is attempting to gain unauthorized access to the system.

rules.title: Events that change user or group information are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: Record events that affect changes to user or group information, including passwords and old passwords if they are used.
rules.impact: Unexpected changes in these files may indicate that the system has been compromised and that an unauthorized user is attempting to hide their activity or compromise additional accounts.

rules.title: Collection of events that modify discretionary access control permissions is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor changes to file permissions, attributes, owners, and groups. The parameters in this section monitor changes to system calls that affect file permissions and attributes. The chmod, fchmod, and fchmodat system calls affect permissions associated with a file. The chown, fchown, fchownat, and lchown system calls affect owner and group attributes on a file. setxattr, lsetxattr, fsetxattr (setting extended file attributes) and removexattr, lremovexattr, fremovexattr (removing extended file attributes) control extended file attributes. In all cases, an audit record will be written only for non-system user IDs (auid >=1000) and will ignore Daemon events (auid = 4294967295). All audit records will be tagged with the identifier "perm_mod".
rules.impact: Monitoring changes in file attributes can alert the system administrator to actions that may indicate attacker activity or a policy violation.

rules.title: Changes to files related to session events are audited is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor session initiation events.
rules.impact: Monitoring these files for changes can alert a system administrator to logons at unusual times, which may indicate attacker activity (that is, a user logging on at a time when they do not normally log on).

rules.title: Login and logout events are monitored is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor logon and logoff events.
rules.impact: Monitoring logon/logoff events can provide the system administrator with information related to attacks against user logon.

rules.title: System calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes are audited is configured
rules.explanation: Monitor use of system calls related to deleting or renaming files and file attributes.
rules.impact: Tracking these calls from unprivileged users can provide the system administrator with evidence that improper deletion of files and file attributes associated with protected files is occurring. Although this audit option will capture all events, system administrators will want to look for specific privileged files that are deleted or modified.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chcon command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful use of the chcon command.
rules.impact: Without generating audit records that relate to the organization's security and mission requirements, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or determine those responsible.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the setfacl command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful or unsuccessful use of the setfacl command.
rules.impact: Without generating audit records that relate to the organization's security and mission requirements, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or determine those responsible.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the chacl command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful or unsuccessful use of the chacl command.
rules.impact: Without generating audit records that relate to the organization's security and mission requirements, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or determine those responsible.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful attempts to use the usermod command are recorded is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must generate audit records for successful/unsuccessful use of the usermod command.
rules.impact: Without generating audit records that relate to the organization's security and mission requirements, it would be difficult to establish, correlate, and investigate incident-related events or determine those responsible.

rules.title: Kernel module loading and unloading events are collected is configured
rules.explanation: Audit loading and unloading of kernel modules. The programs insmod (install a kernel module), rmmod (remove a kernel module), and modprobe (a more sophisticated program for loading and unloading modules, as well as some other functions) control module loading and unloading. The system calls init_module (load a module) and delete_module (delete a module) control module loading and unloading. Any execution of module load/unload programs and system calls generates an audit record with the identifier "modules".
rules.impact: Monitoring use of insmod, rmmod, and modprobe can provide system administrators evidence that an unauthorized user loaded or unloaded a kernel module, which may compromise system security. Monitoring the init_module and delete_module system calls will also record attempts by an unauthorized user to use another program to load and unload modules.

rules.title: The audit configuration is immutable is configured
rules.explanation: Configure system audit so that audit rules cannot be changed using auditctl. Setting the "-e 2" flag forces audit into immutable mode. Audit changes can be made only when the system is rebooted.
rules.impact: In immutable mode, unauthorized users cannot make changes to the audit system to potentially conceal malicious activity and then restore the audit rules. Users are likely to notice a system reboot, and this may alert administrators to an attempt to make unauthorized audit changes.

rules.title: The running configuration and the on-disk configuration are the same is configured
rules.explanation: The audit system has both on-disk and current configuration. These configuration parameters may differ.
rules.impact: Differences between the currently running configuration and what is on disk can cause unexpected problems or create a false impression of compliance.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Rsyslog software is recommended in environments where journald does not meet operational requirements.
rules.impact: Rsyslog security improvements, such as connection-oriented log transport (that is, TCP), the ability to log in database format, and encryption of log data in transit to a central log server, justify installing and configuring the package.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled
rules.explanation: If the rsyslog service is not enabled, the system may default to using syslogd or log by other means.
rules.impact: If the rsyslog service is not enabled, the system may default to using syslogd or log by other means.

rules.title: Default rsyslog file permissions are configured
rules.explanation: Rsyslog will create log files that do not yet exist on the system. This setting controls which permissions are applied to those newly created files. The $FileCreateMode parameter specifies the file creation mode in which rsyslogd creates new files. If not specified, the value 0644 is used.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that log files have the correct permissions to enable archiving and protection of sensitive data.

rules.title: Rsyslog is configured to send logs to a remote log host
rules.explanation: The rsyslog utility supports sending collected logs to a running remote host or receiving messages from remote hosts, reducing administrative overhead.
rules.impact: Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker obtains root access on the local system, they can forge or delete log data stored locally.

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to receive logs from a remote client is configured
rules.explanation: RSyslog supports receiving messages from remote hosts, thus acting as a log server. Clients must not receive data from other hosts.
rules.impact: If the client is also configured to receive data, turning it into a server, the client system operates outside its operational boundaries.

rules.title: Cron daemon is enabled
rules.explanation: The cron daemon is used to run jobs on the system.
rules.impact: Although the system may not have user jobs that need to run, the system has maintenance jobs that may include security monitoring that needs to run. If another task-scheduling method is not used, cron is used to run them and should be enabled and running.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/crontab is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/crontab file is used by cron to manage its own jobs. The commands in this item ensure that root is the user and group owner of the file, and that only the owner can access the file.
rules.impact: This file contains information about which system jobs are executed by cron. Write access to these files may give unprivileged users an opportunity to elevate their privileges. Read access to these files may give users insight into the system jobs that are running on the system and provide them an opportunity to obtain unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.hourly is configured
rules.explanation: This directory contains system cron jobs that need to run hourly. Files in this directory cannot be modified by the crontab command; instead they are edited by system administrators using a text editor.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.daily is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.daily directory contains system cron jobs that need to run daily. Files in this directory cannot be modified by the crontab command; instead they are edited by system administrators using a text editor.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.weekly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains system cron jobs that need to run weekly. Files in this directory cannot be modified by the crontab command; instead they are edited by system administrators using a text editor.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.monthly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains system cron jobs that need to run weekly. Files in this directory cannot be modified by the crontab command; instead they are edited by system administrators using a text editor.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/cron.d is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory contains system cron jobs that should run similarly to hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly jobs from /etc/crontab, but require more granular control of their execution. Files in this directory cannot be modified by the crontab command; instead they are edited by system administrators using a text editor.
rules.impact: Granting write access to this directory to unprivileged users can provide them a means to obtain unauthorized elevated privileges. Granting read access to this directory can give an unprivileged user an understanding of how to obtain elevated privileges or bypass audit controls.

rules.title: Access to /cron is permitted only for authorized users
rules.explanation: If cron is installed on the system, configure /etc/cron.allow to permit specific users to use these services. If /etc/cron.allow does not exist, /etc/cron.deny is checked. Any user not listed in these files may use cron. After removing the deny file, only users in /etc/cron.allow can use cron.
rules.impact: On many systems, only the system administrator is authorized to schedule cron jobs. Using the cron.allow file to control who can run cron jobs enforces this policy. It is easier to manage an allow list than a deny list. On a deny list, you may add a user ID to the system and forget to add it to the deny files.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file contains configuration specifications for sshd. The command below sets the file owner and group to root.
rules.impact: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file must be protected from unauthorized modification by unprivileged users.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/ssh/sshd_config are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file contains configuration specifications for sshd.
rules.impact: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file must be protected from unauthorized modification by unprivileged users.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH key files are configured
rules.explanation: The SSH private key is one of the two files used in SSH public-key authentication. In this authentication method, possession of the private key is confirmation of identity. Only the private key that corresponds to the public key will authenticate successfully. Private keys must be stored and handled carefully, and copies of the private key must not be distributed.
rules.impact: If an unauthorized user obtains the SSH host private key file, the host may be compromised.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host public key files are configured
rules.explanation: An SSH public key is one of two files used in SSH public key authentication. In this authentication method, the public key is the key that can be used to verify digital signatures generated using the corresponding private key. Only the public key corresponding to the private key will be able to successfully authenticate.
rules.impact: If the host public key file is modified by an unauthorized user, the SSH service may be compromised.

rules.title: SSH access is restricted
rules.explanation: There are several options for restricting user and group access to the system over SSH. It is recommended to use at least one of the following: AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, DenyGroups.
rules.impact: Restricting which users can remotely access the system via SSH will help ensure that only authorized users have access to the system.

rules.title: SSH LogLevel is set to INFO is configured
rules.explanation: The INFO level is the baseline level at which only SSH user logon actions are recorded. In many situations, such as incident response, it is important to determine when a particular user was active on the system. A logoff record can exclude those users who disconnected, which helps narrow the field. The VERBOSE level indicates that logon and logoff actions, as well as the key fingerprint for any SSH key used to log on, will be recorded. This information is important for SSH key management, especially in legacy environments.
rules.impact: SSH provides several logging levels with varying degrees of detail. DEBUG is strongly discouraged except strictly for debugging SSH communications, because it provides so much data that it is difficult to identify important security information. INFO is the baseline level that records only SSH user login activity. In many situations, such as incident response, it is important to determine when a particular user was active on the system. A logout record can eliminate those users who have disconnected, which helps narrow the field.

rules.title: SSH PAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface. If set to "yes", this will enable PAM authentication using the ChallengeResponseAuthentication and PasswordAuthentication directives in addition to PAM account and session module processing for all authentication types.
rules.impact: If the usePAM parameter is set to yes, PAM correctly works with account and session types. This is important if you want to restrict access to services based on IP, time, or other account factors. In addition, you can ensure that users inherit certain environment variables at logon or deny access to the server.

rules.title: SSH root login is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitRootLogin parameter specifies whether the root user can log in via ssh. The default is "no".
rules.impact: Disallowing root login via SSH requires system administrators to authenticate using their individual account and then switch to root via sudo or su. This in turn provides a clear audit trail in the event of a security incident.

rules.title: SSH HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies whether authentication via trusted hosts through user .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv, together with successful client host public-key authentication, is permitted. This option applies only to SSH protocol version 2.
rules.impact: Even if .rhosts files are ineffective when support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use .rhosts files in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.

rules.title: SSH PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitEmptyPasswords parameter specifies whether the SSH server permits authentication with empty password strings.
rules.impact: Denying remote shell access to accounts with an empty password reduces the likelihood of unauthorized access to the system.

rules.title: SSH PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: The PermitUserEnvironment parameter allows users to present environment options to the ssh daemon.
rules.impact: Allowing users to set environment variables via the SSH daemon can potentially allow users to bypass security measures (for example, setting an execution path in which ssh executes Trojan programs).

rules.title: SSH IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Setting this parameter requires users to enter a password when authenticating with ssh.

rules.title: SSH X11 forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: The X11Forwarding parameter provides the ability to tunnel X11 traffic over the connection to enable remote graphical sessions.
rules.impact: Disable X11 forwarding unless there is an operational requirement to use X11 applications directly. There is a small risk that remote X11 servers of users who logged in via SSH with X11 forwarding may be compromised by other users on the X11 server. Note that even if X11 forwarding is disabled, users can always set up their own forwarding servers.

rules.title: SSH warning banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted. By default, no banner is displayed.
rules.impact: Banners are used to warn connecting users of the site-specific policy regarding connection.

rules.title: SSH MaxAuthTries is set to 4 or less is configured
rules.explanation: The MaxAuthTries parameter specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts permitted for a single connection. When the login failure counter reaches half of this value, error messages detailing the login failure are written to the system log file.
rules.impact: Setting MaxAuthTries to a low value minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. The recommended value is 4.

rules.title: SSH LoginGraceTime is set to one minute or less
rules.explanation: The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication to the SSH server. The longer the grace period, the more unauthenticated connections may remain open. As with other session controls in this section, the grace period should be limited according to organizational constraints to ensure service availability for required access.
rules.impact: Setting a smaller value for LoginGraceTime minimizes the risk of successful brute-force attacks against the SSH server. It also limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections.

rules.title: SSH idle timeout interval is configured
rules.explanation: The ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters control SSH session timeouts. When the ClientAliveInterval variable is set, ssh sessions that have no activity for the specified period of time are terminated. When the ClientAliveCountMax variable is set, sshd will send client alive messages at each ClientAliveInterval. When the number of consecutive client alive messages is sent without a response from the client, the ssh session is terminated.
rules.impact: The absence of a timeout value associated with a connection may allow an unauthorized user to access another user's ssh session (for example, a user leaves their computer and does not lock the screen). Setting a timeout value at least reduces this risk.

rules.title: Sudo or sudo-ldap is installed is configured
rules.explanation: Sudo allows an authorized user to run a command as the superuser or another user, as specified in the security policy.
rules.impact: Sudo supports a plugin architecture for security policy and I/O logging. Third parties can develop and distribute their own policies and I/O logging plugins to work seamlessly with the sudo interface. The default security policy is sudoers, which is configured using the /etc/sudoers file and any entries in /etc/sudoers.d. The security policy determines what privileges a user has to run sudo. The policy may require users to authenticate with a password or another authentication mechanism. If authentication is required, sudo will terminate if the user password is not entered within a configurable timeout. This restriction is policy-specific.
rules.scope: One of the sudo or sudo-ldap packages when running dpkg-query -W

rules.title: Sudo can execute other commands only from a pseudoterminal is configured
rules.explanation: Sudo can be configured to run only from a pseudo-terminal (pseudo-pty).
rules.impact: Attackers can use sudo to launch a malicious program that forks a background process remaining even after the main program has finished executing.
rules.scope: Parameter in /etc/sudoers or in files in /etc/sudoers.d/

rules.title: The sudo log file exists is configured
rules.explanation: Sudo can use its own log file.
rules.impact: The sudo log file simplifies auditing of sudo commands.
rules.scope: Parameter in /etc/sudoers or in files in /etc/sudoers.d/

rules.title: Users must provide a password for privilege escalation is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must be configured so that users are required to enter a password to elevate privileges.
rules.impact: Without re-authentication, users may access resources or perform tasks for which they are not authorized. When operating systems provide the ability to escalate capabilities, it is critical that the user re-authenticate.

rules.title: Re-authentication for privilege elevation is not disabled globally is configured
rules.explanation: The operating system must be configured so that users must re-authenticate to elevate privileges.
rules.impact: Without re-authentication, users may access resources or perform tasks for which they are not authorized. When operating systems provide the ability to escalate capabilities, it is critical that the user re-authenticate.

rules.title: The sudo authentication timeout is configured correctly
rules.explanation: Sudo caches used credentials for 5 minutes by default. This is done for ease of use when multiple administrative tasks must be performed. The timeout can be changed in accordance with local security policy.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized privileged access as another user.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo, which provides more granular control over privileged access.
