Typically, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in /etc/pam.d/su, the su command will allow only users in specified groups to execute su. This group should be empty to reinforce the use of sudo for privileged access.
rules.impact: Restricting use of su and using sudo instead gives system administrators better control over user privilege elevation for privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and auditing mechanism because it can log every command executed via sudo, whereas su can record only that the user executed the su program.

rules.title: Authselect includes with-faillock is configured
rules.explanation: The pam_faillock.so module maintains a list of failed authentication attempts for each user during a given interval and locks the account if there have been many consecutive failed authentications. It stores failure records in per-user files in a directory.
rules.impact: Locking user identifiers after n failed login attempts reduces the risk of password brute-force attacks against your systems.

rules.title: Password creation requirements is configured
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality.so module checks password strength. It verifies that the password is not a dictionary word, has a specified length, contains a set of character classes (for example, alphabetic, digit, and so on), and more. Definitions of pam_pwquality.so parameters: try_first_pass - retrieve the password from the previous stacked PAM module. If it is unavailable, prompt the user for the password; retry = 3 - allow 3 attempts before returning an error. The following parameters are set in the /etc/security/pwquality.conf file: minlen = 14 - the password must be at least 14 characters; dcredit = -1 - require at least one digit; ucredit = -1 - require at least one uppercase character; ocredit = -1 - require at least one special character; lcredit = -1 - require at least one lowercase character. The settings shown above are one possible policy. Change these values to match your organization's password policies.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect systems from compromise.

rules.title: Lockouts for failed password attempts is configured
rules.explanation: Lock out users after n consecutive failed logon attempts. These settings are typically configured using the pam_faillock.so module. In some environments it may be possible to continue using the pam_tally2.so module, where this older method may simplify automation in mixed environments. Set the lockout number in the deny = policy in effect at your site. unlock_time = _n_ is the number of seconds the account remains locked after the number of attempts configured in deny = _n_ has been reached.
rules.impact: Locking users after n consecutive failed login attempts reduces the likelihood of a password brute-force attack against your systems.
rules.scope: deny and unlock_time parameters in /etc/pam.d/password-auth and /etc/pam.d/system-auth

rules.title: Password reuse restrictions
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file stores users' old passwords and can be used to verify that users are not reusing recent passwords.
rules.impact: Preventing users from reusing their last 5 passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can guess a password.

rules.title: The password hashing algorithm is SHA-512 is configured
rules.explanation: Change password hashing from md5 to sha512 (a much stronger hashing algorithm). All existing accounts will need to change their passwords to update stored hashes to the new algorithm.
rules.impact: The SHA-512 algorithm provides much stronger hashing than MD5, which provides additional system protection by increasing the effort required for an attacker to successfully determine passwords.

rules.title: Password lifetime does not exceed 90 days
rules.explanation: The PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to prevent users from changing their password until a minimum number of days have elapsed since the user's last password change.
rules.impact: The time during which an attacker can use compromised credentials, or successfully compromise credentials using an online brute-force attack, is limited by password age. Therefore, reducing the maximum password lifetime also reduces the attacker's window of opportunity.

rules.title: The minimum number of days between password changes is 7 or more
rules.explanation: The PASS_MIN_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to prevent users from changing their password until a minimum number of days have elapsed since the user last changed their password.
rules.impact: By limiting password-change frequency, an administrator can prevent users from repeatedly changing their password in an attempt to bypass password-reuse controls.

rules.title: Lock inactive passwords
rules.explanation: User accounts that have been inactive for a specified period can be automatically disabled.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts pose a threat to system security because users do not log on to notice failed logon attempts or other anomalies.

rules.title: The password change date is not expired for all users is configured
rules.explanation: All users must have a password change date in the past.
rules.impact: If a user's recorded password change date has not yet occurred, they may bypass any configured password expiration.

rules.title: System accounts are secured is configured
rules.explanation: Most distributions include a number of accounts used to manage applications that are not intended to provide an interactive shell.
rules.impact: It is important to Ensure that accounts not used by regular users cannot be used to provide an interactive shell. By default, most distributions set an invalid string in the password field for these accounts, but it is also recommended that the shell field in the password file be set to the nologin shell. This prevents the account from potentially being used to run any commands.

rules.title: User shell timeout
rules.explanation: TMOUT by default defines the shell idle timeout for users. The TMOUT value is measured in seconds.
rules.impact: Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized access to another user's shell session that has been left unattended. It also terminates an idle session and frees resources associated with that session.

rules.title: Default group for the root account GID 0
rules.explanation: The usermod command can be used to specify which group the root user belongs to. This affects permissions of files created by the root user.
rules.impact: Using GID 0 for the root account helps prevent accidental access to files with root permissions by unprivileged users.

rules.title: Default user umask value
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine the access permissions of newly created directories and files. In Linux, the default permissions for any newly created directory are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx), and for any newly created file are 0666 (rw-rw-rw-). Umask modifies the default Linux permissions by restricting (masking) those permissions. Users who want their files and directories to be readable by other users by default may choose a different default umask by inserting a umask command into the standard shell configuration files (.profile, .bashrc, etc.) in their home directories.
rules.impact: Setting a secure default umask ensures that users make a conscious choice regarding file access permissions. A permissive umask value can result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written by unauthorized users.

rules.title: The sticky bit is set on all world-writable directories is configured
rules.explanation: Setting the sticky bit on world-writable directories prevents users from deleting or renaming files in that directory that they do not own.
rules.impact: This feature prevents deletion or renaming of files in world-writable directories (such as /tmp) that are owned by another user.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file contains user-account information that is used by many system utilities and therefore must be readable for those utilities to function.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that the /etc/passwd file is protected from unauthorized write access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow file is used to store user account information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to the /etc/shadow file, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed password to crack it. Other security information stored in the /etc/shadow file (for example, expiration) may also be useful for undermining user accounts.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file contains the list of all valid groups defined on the system.
rules.impact: The /etc/group file should be protected from unauthorized modification by unprivileged users, but should be readable because this information is used by many unprivileged programs.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/gshadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file is used to store group information that is critical to the security of these accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/gshadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed password to crack it.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/passwd- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd- file contains backup user account information.
rules.impact: It is very important to ensure that the /etc/passwd- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/passwd- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd- file contains backup user account information.
rules.impact: It is very important to ensure that the /etc/passwd- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/shadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow- file is used to store backup user account information that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: It is critical to protect /etc/shadow- from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed either accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: Permissions for /etc/gshadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow- file is used to store group information that is critical to the security of these accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.
rules.impact: It is very important to ensure that the /etc/gshadow- file is protected from unauthorized access. Although it is protected by default, file permissions may be changed accidentally or through malicious activity.

rules.title: There are no world-writable files
rules.explanation: Unix systems support variable settings for controlling access to files. World-writable files are the least secure.
rules.impact: Data in world-writable files can be modified and compromised by any user on the system. Writable files may also indicate a poorly written script or program that could potentially cause a more serious system integrity compromise.

rules.title: No unused files or directories exist
rules.explanation: Sometimes when administrators remove users from the password file, they forget to remove all files belonging to those users from the system.
rules.impact: A new user who is assigned a user or group identifier of deleted users may eventually "own" those files and thus have greater access to the system than intended.

rules.title: No unused files or directories exist
rules.explanation: Sometimes when administrators remove users from the password file, they forget to remove all files belonging to those users from the system.
rules.impact: A new user who is assigned a user or group identifier of deleted users may eventually "own" those files and thus have greater access to the system than intended.

rules.title: Audit SUID executable files
rules.explanation: The file owner can set permissions to run the file with the owner's or group's permissions even if the user running the program is not the owner or a group member. The most common reason for an SUID program is to allow users to perform functions (such as changing their password) that require superuser privileges.
rules.impact: There are valid reasons for SUID programs, but it is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate.

rules.title: Audit SGID executable files
rules.explanation: The file owner can set permissions to run the file with the owner's or group's permissions even if the user running the program is not the owner or a member of the group. The most common reason for using an SGID program is to allow users to perform functions (for example, changing their password) that require superuser privileges.
rules.impact: There are legitimate reasons for SGID programs, but it is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate. Review the files returned by the audit action and check whether system binaries have an md5 checksum that differs from the one in the package. This indicates that the binary may have been replaced.

rules.title: Password fields are not empty
rules.explanation: An account with an empty password field means anyone can log on as that user without providing a password.
rules.impact: All accounts must have passwords or be locked to prevent use of the account by an unauthorized user.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although the useradd program will not allow you to create a duplicate user identifier (UID), an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the UID field.
rules.impact: Users must be assigned unique UIDs to ensure proper access protection.

rules.title: No duplicate usernames exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although useradd will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: No duplicate usernames exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although useradd will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist is configured
rules.explanation: Although groupadd will not allow you to create a duplicate group name, an administrator can manually edit /etc/group and change a group name.
rules.impact: If a group is assigned a duplicate group name, it will create and access files with the first GID for that group in /etc/group. Essentially, the GID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: Integrity of the root PATH is configured
rules.explanation: The root user can execute any command on the system and can be tricked into unintentionally executing programs if PATH is not set correctly.
rules.impact: Including the current working directory (.) or another writable directory in the root executable path increases the likelihood that an attacker can obtain superuser access by causing an administrator running as root to execute a Trojan program.

rules.title: Root is the only UID 0 account
rules.explanation: Any account with UID 0 has superuser privileges on the system.
rules.impact: This access should be restricted to the root account by default and only from the system console. Administrative access should be performed through an unprivileged account using an approved mechanism.

rules.title: Local interactive users own their home directories is configured
rules.explanation: A user's home directory is space defined for a specific user to set local environment variables and store personal files.
rules.impact: Because the user is responsible for files stored in the user's home directory, the user should own that directory.

rules.title: Iptables is installed and enabled is configured
rules.explanation: The iptables and iptables-services packages provide an iptables-based firewall and rule persistence. To filter network traffic, the firewall must be installed and active.
rules.impact: The absence of an installed and enabled firewall leaves the system without network filtering, which increases the attack surface.

rules.title: Syslog-ng or rsyslog is installed, enabled, and forwards logs to a remote host is configured
rules.explanation: The logging service (syslog-ng or rsyslog) must be installed, enabled, and configured to send logs to a remote log-collection host. Verification is performed using OR logic between syslog-ng and rsyslog.
rules.impact: The absence of centralized log collection hinders incident investigation and allows an attacker to conceal traces locally.

rules.title: OSSEC is installed and running, or that AIDE integrity checking is configured
rules.explanation: A host-based integrity and intrusion detection capability must be present: OSSEC HIDS is installed and running, or regular AIDE file system integrity checking is configured. The check is performed using OR logic.
rules.impact: Lack of file integrity monitoring reduces the chance of timely detection of unauthorized changes to system files.
rules.scope: ossec package; root cron job for ossec; aide package/job

rules.title: Strong hashing algorithms are used to store passwords is configured
rules.explanation: The password field in /etc/shadow contains the hashing algorithm identifier: $6$ (SHA-512), $5$ (SHA-256), $2$ (Blowfish/bcrypt), $1$ (MD5). Weak algorithms (MD5) are not permitted.
rules.impact: Using weak password hashing algorithms (MD5) makes password recovery easier if the /etc/shadow file is compromised.

rules.title: Time synchronization (chrony or ntpdate) is installed, enabled, and active is configured
rules.explanation: For correct logging and cryptography operation, the system must synchronize time. The presence, enablement, and activity of one of the time-synchronization facilities (chrony, ntp, ntpdate) is verified using OR logic.
rules.impact: System time desynchronization breaks correlation of events in logs and may cause certificate validation failures.

rules.title: Log files in /var/log are owned by root and have permissions of 0640/0750 or more restrictive is configured
rules.explanation: Log files in /var/log must be owned by user root, group root (or a system group), and have permissions no more permissive than 0640 for files and 0750 for directories.
rules.impact: Excessive permissions on log files allow unprivileged users to read or modify log records.
